title: NVIDIA Refutes RTX 5090 Discontinuation Rumors; Jeff Fisher Confirms Flagship GPU Still Shipping
body:
NVIDIA has publicly refuted circulating rumors that its flagship Blackwell‑based RTX 5090 graphics card will be discontinued, with senior executive Jeff Fisher confirming that the high‑end GPU will remain in production despite ongoing supply constraints that have driven retail prices north of $5,000. The clarification comes amid a wave of speculative reports from several Taiwanese media outlets suggesting that the company was preparing to phase out the RTX 5090 in favor of newer, unreleased models.

The denial was issued through an official statement from NVIDIA’s corporate communications team, which emphasized that the RTX 5090 “continues to be a cornerstone of our product lineup” and that the company “remains fully committed to supporting the Blackwell architecture for the foreseeable future.” Fisher, who oversees product strategy for the GeForce division, echoed the message in a brief interview, noting that the GPU’s performance envelope and feature set still align with the demands of professional creators, AI researchers, and extreme gamers who require the utmost computational power.

Supply chain pressures have been a persistent challenge for the semiconductor industry since the pandemic, and NVIDIA’s premium segment is feeling the impact acutely. The RTX 5090, built on the 5‑nm process and equipped with a staggering 48 GB of GDDR6X memory, has seen demand outstrip the limited inventory that manufacturers can allocate. Retailers worldwide have reported price tags well above the card’s suggested retail price, prompting speculation that NVIDIA might pull the product to curb market volatility. However, analysts at IDC and TrendForce argue that the decision to keep the RTX 5090 in production is a strategic move to preserve the brand’s high‑end reputation while the company ramps up capacity for its upcoming Ada‑Lovelace and future Blackwell‑derived offerings.

Industry observers also point out that the RTX 5090 serves a niche but lucrative segment that drives much of NVIDIA’s revenue from the professional and data‑center markets. The GPU’s advanced tensor cores and ray‑tracing capabilities are leveraged in AI training workloads, scientific simulations, and high‑resolution content creation. Pulling the card could disrupt existing pipelines for enterprises that have already integrated the hardware into their workflows. By maintaining the product’s availability, NVIDIA safeguards those relationships and avoids the reputational risk associated with abrupt product withdrawals.

The controversy underscores a broader tension between consumer expectations and the realities of semiconductor manufacturing. While enthusiasts eagerly await next‑generation GPUs, the industry’s capacity constraints mean that even flagship products may experience prolonged lead times and inflated secondary‑market prices. NVIDIA’s reassurance about the RTX 5090 may help stabilize the market, but it does not resolve the underlying supply bottlenecks that have plagued the sector for years. Analysts suggest that the company’s upcoming silicon refreshes, combined with investments in new fab capacity by partners like TSMC, could gradually ease the pressure, though a full normalization may not occur until 2025.

Looking ahead, NVIDIA’s commitment to the RTX 5090 signals that the company intends to sustain its premium tier while it fine‑tunes the rollout of newer architectures. Customers and partners can expect continued driver updates, performance optimizations, and support for emerging software standards. As the GPU market continues to grapple with demand‑supply imbalances, NVIDIA’s stance may serve as a bellwether for how other manufacturers handle their flagship offerings—balancing scarcity‑driven hype with the need for reliable product continuity.
